passage: I'm Ujjwal, and this is my little brother Varun at the park last Sunday. Varun was telling the flower seller about the ladybird he found. "It was red, and it had, and it went on my..." Then the ice-cream cart bell rang. Varun turned and ran, mid-sentence, leaving the sentence hanging. The flower seller blinked and then laughed. I don't know what Varun felt, but it looked like the bell simply pulled him away. I called after him, "Varun, say bye first!" He skidded, turned and shouted, "Bye, uncle! I'll finish later!" and dashed off. The flower seller waved.

qa.q: What was Varun telling the flower seller about?
qa.a: A ladybird that Varun found.

qa.q: What do you think Varun was feeling when the ice-cream cart bell rang?
qa.a: Probably excited, though Ujjwal cannot be sure; the bell pulled Varun away mid-sentence, so the pull looked stronger than the wish to finish the story.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that helped, and what small skill did Varun show?
qa.a: Ujjwal called out "say bye first," and Varun turned back to say "Bye, uncle! I'll finish later!" before running off.

qa.q: How might the flower seller feel when Varun ran off mid-sentence?
qa.a: Surprised for a moment, then amused, since the seller blinked and laughed and then waved goodbye.

grounding: A child runs off mid-sentence when something more interesting appears, and a reminder to say bye teaches a small social skill.

passage:
Monday: Tarun was telling Mama Vinita about the school rabbit when the ice-cream van's tune played outside. Tarun dashed to the door, and the story stopped.
Wednesday: Mama Vinita, leaving the kitchen, said, "I'm going to hang the clothes now. Bye for a bit! I'll be on the terrace." Tarun watched and waved.
Friday: Tarun was halfway through a story about the cricket ball when a kite passed the window. Tarun stopped, looked at Mama, and said, "Bye, Mama, I'm going to see the kite!" Then ran. Mama Vinita called, "Thank you for telling me! Finish later?" Tarun nodded, smiling.

qa.q: What was Tarun telling Mama Vinita about on Monday?
qa.a: The school rabbit.

qa.q: What did Tarun feel when the ice-cream van's tune played on Monday?
qa.a: Excitement so strong that the story was forgotten. Tarun dashed to the door without finishing.

qa.q: What did Mama Vinita do on Wednesday that helped Tarun learn?
qa.a: Mama Vinita showed how to leave politely by saying "I'm going to hang the clothes now. Bye for a bit!" before going.

qa.q: How might Mama Vinita have felt on Friday when Tarun said bye before running off?
qa.a: Pleased. The new habit had started, and Mama answered with thanks and an offer to finish the story later.

grounding: A child who runs off mid-sentence learns from an adult who models saying bye or I will go now.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Monday.
During free play, Harsha (5) was telling Minakshi about her new cat: "And she has white socks and she sleeps on my—" Then the bubble machine started in the corner, and Harsha ran off mid-sentence. Minakshi stood there, looking puzzled and a bit sad.
I brought Harsha back gently. "When you want to go, you can say, 'Bye, I'm going to the bubbles!'" I said it with her. She said, "Bye Minakshi, I'm going to the bubbles!" and Minakshi waved.
I'll practise "bye, I'm going now" with the whole class this week.

qa.q: What started in the corner?
qa.a: The bubble machine.

qa.q: Why did Harsha run off mid-sentence?
qa.a: Harsha was excited and distracted by the bubbles, and forgot about being in the middle of talking.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that taught Harsha a small social skill?
qa.a: The teacher brought Harsha back and modelled saying 'Bye, I'm going to the bubbles!' together with her.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when Harsha came back to say bye?
qa.a: She probably felt better and included, waving goodbye.

grounding: Shows a young child running off mid-sentence and an adult modelling how to say bye before leaving.

passage: At the village well, Raghav, five, was telling Dolma aunty about his new calf. "She has a white spot and she drinks so much milk and—" The ice-cream cart bell rang down the lane. Raghav turned and ran without another word. Dolma aunty laughed, but Papa called him back. "Raghav, Dolma aunty was listening to you. What do we say when we go?" Raghav thought. "Bye?" "Try: 'I'll go now, bye, aunty!'" Raghav said it, waved, and ran off again. Dolma aunty waved back, smiling.

qa.q: What did Raghav's calf have?
qa.a: A white spot.

qa.q: Why did Raghav run off mid-sentence?
qa.a: He was excited and distracted by the ice-cream cart bell, forgetting he was talking.

qa.q: What did Papa model for Raghav?
qa.a: Papa taught him to say 'I'll go now, bye, aunty!' before leaving.

qa.q: How did Dolma aunty react?
qa.a: She laughed at first and then smiled and waved back, pleased with the proper goodbye.

grounding: Shows a young child running off mid-sentence and a parent modelling a simple goodbye.

passage: In a Beirut courtyard, Dalia, five, was telling her grandmother Clara about her dream. "And the fish could talk, and it said—" A puppy trotted past the gate. Dalia dashed after it. Teta Clara sat with her mouth half-open, then chuckled. Mama called, "Dalia! Come back and say goodbye first." Dalia came back, puffing. Mama crouched. "You can say, 'Teta, I'll finish later, bye!'" Dalia said it and hugged her grandmother. "Bye, Teta!" Then she ran after the puppy.

qa.q: What did Dalia see pass the gate?
qa.a: A puppy.

qa.q: How did Teta Clara feel when Dalia dashed off?
qa.a: She seemed surprised, with her mouth half-open, but also amused, chuckling.

qa.q: What small skill did Mama model?
qa.a: Saying 'Teta, I'll finish later, bye!' before running off, so the conversation ends kindly.

qa.q: How might Teta Clara feel after the hug and goodbye?
qa.a: She would probably feel loved and included, knowing Dalia will finish the story later.

grounding: Shows a young child running off mid-sentence and a parent modelling how to say goodbye first.

passage: At the community library's story corner, Uma was telling Baljeet Aunty about her new sandals. "And they have a flower here, and when I walk they—" Through the window she saw the ice-cream cart. She was gone mid-sentence. Baljeet Aunty waited until Uma came back for her bag. "Uma, when you want to go, you can say, 'I'm going now, bye!' Then I know." Uma thought. "I'm going now, bye!" she tried. "Bye, Uma! Tell me about the flower next time." On Saturday, when her mother came, Uma said it all by herself before she ran.

qa.q: What did Uma see through the window?
qa.a: She saw the ice-cream cart.

qa.q: Why did Uma run off mid-sentence?
qa.a: She got so excited about the ice-cream cart that she forgot she was talking; she wasn't trying to be rude.

qa.q: What did Baljeet Aunty do that taught Uma a new skill?
qa.a: She gave Uma simple words, "I'm going now, bye!", let her try them, and said a warm goodbye back 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Baljeet Aunty when Uma ran off?
qa.a: She may have felt a little cut off and amused, left mid-sentence about the sandals.

grounding: Shows a young child running off mid-sentence and an adult modelling a simple goodbye she can use next time.
